topic.title: Sanctuary cities
topic.proposition: Cities should limit their local police's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: I think the bigger threat to public safety is broken trust. When people fear that any contact with local police could lead to a neighbor or family member being deported, they stop reporting crimes and stop acting as witnesses, and that makes whole neighborhoods less safe. Local police aren't trained or funded to do federal immigration work, and pulling them into it takes time away from solving actual local crimes. I'd rather see police stick to their core job than serve as an extension of a separate federal agency.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I understand the trust concern, but in my view the deeper issue is accountability. When cities limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, they're essentially deciding which federal laws deserve respect, and that chips away at the rule of law more broadly. If someone here illegally commits a crime, I don't see why local police shouldn't share that information with federal authorities. Public safety has to come first, and I worry these limiting policies send a message that consequences are optional depending on where you live.

messages.author: Participant A
messages.text: That's a fair point about accountability, and I won't deny that some communities want clearer consequences for serious crimes. But I think there's a real difference between everyday policing and using local police as an enforcement arm for federal immigration matters. My worry is that even narrow cooperation tends to expand over time through pressure and practice, and once that starts, immigrant residents notice and pull back from all contact with police, not just the risky kind. I'd rather cities draw a firm boundary now than try to walk it back after trust is already broken.

messages.author: Participant B
messages.text: I hear that worry about mission creep, but I think allowing broad limits on cooperation creates its own avoidable risk, especially when it means local police can't flag someone already in custody for a serious offense. That isn't door to door enforcement, it's basic information sharing about people already inside the system. I'd rather see cities allow cooperation in serious cases while limiting it elsewhere, instead of cutting communication off entirely by policy. This is the claim I am relying on.
